neighbours.label: Mathematical prose about inclusion and order relations (subset of, partial order, reflexive/antisymmetric/transitive, set difference), vs math prose about arithmetic or everyday uses of 'set' and 'subset'
fire: In lattice theory, the relation of inclusion between subsets is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive.
Since every element of X belongs to Y, X is a subset of Y, and Y is in turn a subset of Z.
A total order is a partial order in which any two elements are comparable.
The empty set is a subset of every set, and every set is a subset of itself.
Therefore the relation is antisymmetric: if a precedes b and b precedes a, then a equals b.
Let S be a proper subset of T, so T minus S is nonempty.
Equality of sets is defined by mutual inclusion: each must be a subset of the other.
Under the divisibility order, 1 precedes every positive integer and the order is transitive.
quiet: In arithmetic, the sum of two odd numbers is always an even number.
Since each apple costs two dollars, five apples cost ten dollars in total.
A prime number has exactly two divisors, one and the number itself.
The kids set the table while their mother finished cooking dinner.
Only a small subset of the voters showed up at the town meeting.
Multiply both sides of the equation by three to clear the fraction.
The chef picked a subset of herbs from the garden for the sauce.
The area of a rectangle is its length multiplied by its width.

predictions: Sentences stating inclusion or order-relation properties reach 0.2-0.7; arithmetic statements and everyday 'set'/'subset' stay under 0.1.
notes: Card top examples are HTML-entity tables (nsubseteq, NotSupersetEqual, Precedes), a partial order, issubset, set difference. Probe: 'reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive' 0.716, 'A is a subset of B ... subset of C' 0.418, set difference 0.213, partial order 0.182, issubset in code 0.044; 'set off' 0.007, 'a subset of the photos' 0.006.
